item.title: California Cancels Talks With Paramount Over Warner Bros. Merger
item.description:
California’s attorney general has canceled a meeting with representatives of Paramount that was scheduled for Monday to begin discussing a settlement of the state’s lawsuit seeking to block Paramount’s proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.

Rob Bonta, the attorney general, called off the meeting late Sunday, accusing Paramount of acting in bad faith. In a statement to The Times, Mr. Bonta accused Paramount of leaking details of a meeting the parties held on Friday.

“Not only did Paramount leak the alleged substance of settlement discussions, but they misrepresented these discussions, demonstrating a lack of good faith,” Mr. Bonta said in the statement. “As soon as Paramount stops playing games and engages sincerely, my office is happy to meet again.”

A spokeswoman for Paramount did not have immediate comment on Monday morning.

The Monday meeting was supposed to be preliminary, and there was never any assurance that it would lead to meaningful negotiations toward a settlement. But the possibility that the two sides could begin moving toward an agreement was seen as something of a breakthrough after Paramount threatened to leave California and Gov. Gavin Newsom expressed a preference for settling the case.

Paramount’s proposed $111 billion purchase of Warner Bros. would create a media giant, combining two major movie studios, multiple streaming services and the news outlets CNN and CBS News. The company, headquartered in Hollywood, would also be a major employer in Los Angeles.

Last month, California led a group of 12 state attorneys general in suing to block the deal, arguing it would create a company with outsize market power in cable television and movie studios.

Mr. Bonta had previously said he would be willing to accept only structural remedies to resolve the lawsuit, which would typically mean requiring the companies to sell off parts of the combined business. Executives are often reluctant to hive off parts of a newly merged company because they have already made financial assumptions about the combined operations.

With a trial scheduled for March, delays could cost the company hundreds of millions of dollars in fees that it must start paying to Warner Bros. shareholders if the deal is not closed by October.

Political pressure has been building for the two sides to reach a resolution. Mayor Karen Bass of Los Angeles last week said disputes over the merger had stalled productions and led to job losses in Hollywood. She called for a “swift and urgent resolution” to the lawsuit.

Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for governor of California, also said this month that he would like to see the lawsuit settled.

Mr. Newsom, who is in his final months as governor of California and considering a run for president in 2028, said on Friday that he took Paramount’s threat to leave the state seriously.

“I’m concerned about the state, our reputation,” he said. “I want to see Hollywood thrive.”

Benjamin Mullin, Lauren Hirsch and Francesca Regalado contributed reporting.

item.title: U.S. Unveils Campaign to Cripple Iran’s Economy, but Offers Few Details
item.description:
The Trump administration on Monday announced what it called its most comprehensive assault to date on Iran’s economy, unveiling a package of measures that are intended to isolate Iran from the rest of the world.

The move is a shift by the United States in favor of confronting Iran with economic warfare as negotiations to end the military conflict continue to sputter. The war with Iran remains a drag on the global economy, one that has pushed energy prices higher and eroded President Trump’s approval ratings.

The Trump administration has billed the effort as the coming of an economic apocalypse for Iran. But the announcement on Monday did not make clear how the measures would further disrupt Iran’s economy or whether they would be severe enough to get Iran to end its nuclear program and allow oil to move freely through the Strait of Hormuz.

Mr. Trump, who carried out a “maximum pressure” campaign against Iran during his first term, enacted a package of measures called Operation Economic Fury aimed at Tehran earlier this year. On Monday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent characterized the announcement as D-Day, but later acknowledged it was more of a warning shot that would begin a period of “quiet diplomacy” with counterparts around the world.

Speaking at the Treasury Department, Mr. Bessent labeled the initiative Operation Economic Outcast, and vowed that the United States would “tighten the noose” around Iran by imposing sanctions on every source or facilitator of its revenue. The campaign is intended to exert pressure on other countries, including potentially China and Russia, that continue to trade with Iran or help it evade U.S. sanctions.

“This is a sustained campaign to collapse every last option for Iran,” Mr. Bessent said. “The campaign we begin today will gather force with every day that follows, and it will not end until this regime stands alone.”

The new Iran sanctions include more than 60 entities, individuals and vessels around the world that allow Iran to procure nuclear and missile technology, Mr. Bessent said. The Treasury Department is also imposing sanctions on Iran related to digital assets, gold and the aviation sectors that Iran uses to help finance its economy.

Mr. Bessent said that waves of additional sanctions, including on a large financial institution, would be announced in the coming days and weeks.

Much of the work of isolating Iran, he added, will take place through private negotiations with other countries to compel them to cut ties with Tehran. The Treasury secretary said that the United States did not have a set timeline for such talks, but that it did not have “infinite patience.” The threat of the new sanctions already appeared to be yielding results, with the United Arab Emirates announcing last week that it is halting all trade and financial transactions with Iran.

The United States has a unique ability to use sanctions as a diplomatic tool because of the status of the dollar as the world’s reserve currency. Because the dollar is used in most of the world’s financial transactions, the Treasury Department has the ability to cut individuals and businesses off from much of the global financial system. However, overuse of these tools has the potential to push countries away from using dollars and could create chaos across the world economy.

Mr. Bessent suggested that the United States was giving other nations an opportunity to sever their relationships with Iran before embarking on broader “secondary” sanctions.

“We are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior,” Mr. Bessent said.

In an acknowledgment that a barrage of new sanctions aimed at countries around the world could have unwanted consequences, Mr. Bessent added: “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?”

The most complicated of the diplomatic negotiations will be with China, which is the largest buyer of Iranian oil and has a financial system that is largely insulated from the threat of U.S. sanctions. Asked about sanctions on Chinese banks, Mr. Bessent said, “No one is above the reach of U.S. sanctions,” but did not address China specifically.

The United States is in a fragile trade truce with China, and its president, Xi Jinping, is expected meet with Mr. Trump next month. The Treasury Department has imposed sanctions on independent Chinese refineries that buy Iranian oil, but it has refrained from imposing large-scale sanctions on Chinese financial institutions that facilitate such transactions.

“Until we see actions against more meaningful countries and companies continuing to trade with Iran, it’s just words,” said Daniel Tannebaum, a partner at Oliver Wyman and senior fellow at the Atlantic Council. “Ideally quiet diplomacy is playing out between Trump and Xi to make a deal to pull China from Iran, but that’s a big question in terms of how much influence President Trump has there.”

Iran’s Foreign Ministry said on Monday that Tehran would not bow to an escalating pressure campaign by the Trump administration, after one of the country’s top security chiefs threatened reprisals against countries that joined the United States’ “economic war.”

Esmaeil Baghaei, the Foreign Ministry spokesman, said on Monday that the Trump administration was merely “repeating methods that have proven unsuccessful” in the past.

“Iran will certainly use all multilateral capacities to counter economic sanctions,” he told reporters at a news conference. Ordinary Iranian civilians, he added, would bear the cost of U.S. sanctions.

item.title: In West Texas, Trump’s Border Wall Collides With Latino History
item.description:
Out in Far West Texas, a heavy bronze bell once tolled, calling congregants from both sides of the U.S.-Mexico border to worship at a small adobe church.

The bell and the Catholic church in Ruidosa are hallmarks of an era when Mexican and American border communities lived as one. But nearly three generations ago, parishioners moved away from the tiny town. One of the church’s twin towers toppled. The bell disappeared.

Local volunteers have begun restoring the church, El Corazón Sagrado de la Iglesia de Jesús. They view it as one of the last vestiges of a shared history along a southwestern landscape that is as Indigenous, Spanish and Mexican as it is American. Fortifying its walls and twin towers means that perhaps the bell could ring again.

Now their work faces a new danger: President Trump’s border wall. The church is one of dozens of historical sites across the Southwest threatened by the construction. In Arizona, portions of a 1,000-year-old etching in the earth have been bulldozed. In Texas, work is endangering ancient cave murals and landmarks on the Underground Railroad.

“If you value a people’s worth and contributions, then you preserve their history in textbooks and curriculums,” the historian Trinidad Gonzales said. “You would preserve these physical markers.”

Trump administration officials say the wall will go up yards away from the church and help deter violent drug traffickers in one of the most remote parts of the Chihuahuan desert. Preservationists, though, warn that the relentless vibrations of the construction threaten the church’s fragile structural integrity.

To historians and border residents, the administration’s construction plans, alongside a campaign to deport thousands of immigrants, amount to uprooting centuries of Mexican and Latino American history and presence.

The 110-year journey of the church and its bell is a story of displacement and migration, of being lost and improbably found, and of artists, historians and community residents who have gone to great lengths to bake and haul adobe bricks, bail the bell out of a Marfa jail and reclaim a piece of lost past.

El Corazón Sagrado arose during the Mexican Revolution. Hundreds of thousands of Mexicans were migrating north. They opened schools, theaters and newspapers and, in the borderland, they organized against U.S. segregation and anti-Mexican discrimination.

In Ruidosa, a tiny settlement southwest of Marfa, the community built a church. Mexican and Mexican American families from both sides of the river molded clay bricks to raise its mission-style walls and twin towers. From a central wooden gable, they hung its bronze bell.

For nearly 40 years, the bell tolled. It brought people together for weddings, funerals and Sunday masses.

”The church was a center of life,” said Zenaida Maria Nazeri, 77, who was born in Ruidosa and attended its services.

But by the 1950s, a New Mexico dam and a drought had choked the river that sustained Ruidosa’s farmland. Many in the region began to move again. The post office closed. El Sagrado Corazón fell into disrepair, and the Catholic Church officially retired the mission in 1956.

Sometime in the 1960s, the bell finally migrated, too. The front entryway fell after years of winds and rains had eroded its foundation. The great bell crashed to the earth. A family retrieved it and gave it to Johnnie Tucker Chambers, a teacher living in a nearby schoolhouse. She mounted the bell on a wooden stand and used it to call children from both sides of the border to class.

When she left, she took it to her property in nearby Candelaria, where she used it to call her ranch hands to dinner.

Without its bell, the Ruidosa church, named for the Sacred Heart, seemed to lose its own pulse. The building was locked up, its doors and windows boarded up to prevent vandals from scavenging its wooden floor and pews.

By the early 1990s, the left tower had collapsed, and the El Paso Diocese officially ordered the mission demolished.

That stirred something in people.

Historians, church patrons and community residents expressed their outrage in letters to local newspapers and the diocese. County commissioners paused the Catholic Church’s demolition request.

Restoration efforts regained momentum in 2019, not long after Mr. Trump was elected on rallying cries to “build the wall.”

In his second term, the Trump administration has pushed those plans forward, placing El Sagrado Corazón in jeopardy. U.S. Customs and Border Protection did not respond to questions regarding the community concerns about preserving the church and other sacred sites. In federal lawsuits, administration officials argue they have the authority to waive environmental regulations and other legal claims in the interest of tackling drug smuggling and illegal immigration.

Across the Southwest, similar projects have already begun. In California, explosives have blasted Tecate Peak, also known as Kuuchamaa, a mountain sacred to the Kumeyaay people that is on the National Register of Historic Places. In Arizona’s Sonoran Desert, construction crews bulldozed parts of the 1,000-year-old Las Playas Intaglio, a giant fish-shaped image etched into the earth, disturbed sacred burial grounds at Monument Hill and threatened Quitobaquito Springs, a 10,000-year-old desert oasis revered by the Tohono O’odham and Hia-Ced O’odham nations.

Further east in New Mexico, land seizure efforts are targeting church-owned land around Mount Cristo Rey, a 720-foot Catholic pilgrimage site. In Texas, proposed barriers endanger the 6,000-year-old cave murals of the Lower Pecos Canyonlands, Underground Railroad sanctuaries such as the Eli Jackson Cemetery and Jackson Ranch Church, and the 19th-century La Lomita Chapel in Mission.

In West Texas, protests erupted this month as bulldozers cleared terrain in Big Bend National Park and near the site of the Porvenir Massacre, where a force of Texas Rangers, U.S. Cavalry soldiers, and local ranchers rounded up and shot dead15 unarmed Mexican men and boys in 1918.

Last week, Rodney Scott, the U.S. Customs and Border Protection commissioner, paused the construction in Big Bend as he visited the region. He said only patrol roads and vehicle barriers were planned to go through the national park and that his agency was “firmly committed to protecting America, and that includes our national treasures.”

The preservationists of Ruidosa church say that Mr. Scott’s pause is not cause for celebration. Construction of a steel wall is still expected to continue miles up the road, bringing heavy machinery and excavations within yards of the sanctuary. They and local leaders have filed federal lawsuits and have been pushing back with the help of landowners, including some Trump supporters.

For Mike Green, a retired architect who has long lived in West Texas and helps lead the latest restoration campaign, the construction has been especially troubling.

He felt a kinship with the church when he first saw its ruins in 1984. Scavengers had stripped most of its timber, but he was captivated by its adobe arches — among the tallest still standing in Texas — and by the history of the 160 farmworkers buried on a hill just above it.

“Presidio and Ojinaga have had this rich history, and it’s a history of longstanding community cooperation,” he said of the Mexican and American border cities.

In 2020, after years of negotiation, the diocese deeded the property to Friends of the Ruidosa Church, a nonprofit founded by Mr. Green and the archaeologist David Keller. The group resumed the process of making thousands of sun-dried adobe blocks by hand and has worked with restoration and engineering experts to build and install a modular steel tower structure to buttress the church’s right tower.

The group has even found its key missing piece: the bell.

In 2023, Mr. Green happened to lament the lost artifact to his friend, Betty Gaddis, over lunch. Unbeknown to him, Ms. Gaddis, then 90, had been a longtime friend of Ms. Chambers and had once seen the old bell sitting in her Alpine apartment. Within two days, she tracked the bell down — it was sitting in storage in the Presidio County jail in Marfa.

On Oct. 28, 2023, members of the nonprofit gathered to “bail out” the bell. A month later, they trucked it back to Ruidosa for an annual celebration, displaying it on an altar against an art installation and before dozens of glowing candles.

Now it sits in Mr. Green’s Marfa home, waiting to chime across the valley again.

item.title: Farmers Struggle to Get Basic Services From Depleted Agriculture Dept.
item.description:
Mary and Zachariah Ben, farmers in New Mexico, believed they were on the verge of buying the property of their dreams last fall: 47 acres, with enough cropland to grow heirloom corn and a processing facility to expand their organic baby food business.

But the low-interest loan they secured from the Agriculture Department to make the purchase in Aztec, N.M., was on hold for months, first during the government shutdown that lasted until mid-November and then as federal workers left the agency in droves. Only half a dozen loan specialists who could help process their claims remained in the entire state, the couple learned, leaving them in limbo indefinitely and the seller impatient to know whether the agreement would ever go through.

Zachariah Ben, who along with his children is a member of the Navajo Nation, ultimately turned to private lenders instead, and the family absorbed more than $200,000 in interest as a result. “At least we got the land because we could have also lost that, and we would have if we had to wait” on the Agriculture Department, Mary Ben said.

The experience of the Bens, whose aim of providing organic and shelf-stable options for young children appears to align with some of the Trump administration’s stated goals, is not unique. Across the country, farmers and rural residents describe struggling to obtain the basic services the Agriculture Department is meant to offer, including loans and grants, technical assistance and financing for housing and utilities. Sharp attrition under the Trump administration, largely through voluntary resignations and dismissals by the Department of Government Efficiency, have left many of the Agriculture Department’s local offices with skeletal staffing — and, in some counties, with no one at all.

The ripple effects of the Agriculture Department’s depleted work force illustrate how the Trump administration’s mission of shrinking the federal bureaucracy has undercut a competing priority: delivering for farmers, a core political constituency. Strained government resources also risk posing additional challenges for a farm economy that administration officials have described as “dire,” increasing barriers to entry for new farmers who need more assistance, impeding assistance to producers already facing tough economic conditions, and hampering basic services and government aid in the most remote and poorest places.

“All these practical things that make the wheels go around in a community were facilitated by U.S.D.A., and it was with staff who knew how to navigate and had the trust of the local community,” Senator Pete Welch of Vermont, the top Democrat on the Senate subcommittee on rural development, said in an interview. “It’s something that was working, was working well, and was very cost-efficient. And now it is being demolished.”

Trump administration officials have defended the staffing cuts as voluntary and necessary to trim a bloated agency.

“We don’t have the money in our budget to pay for all of the employees that were hired in the prior administration,” Stephen Vaden, the deputy secretary of agriculture, said in a congressional hearing in July. He emphasized that the reductions were “voluntary decisions made by individual employees who chose, with the information that the agency provided to them, to seek a new career elsewhere.”

Overall, more than 20,000 workers out of more than 110,000 left the Agriculture Department through the first half of 2025, according to an inspector general report. Recently obtained data showed that the Farm Service Agency, a division whose approval the Bens sought in applying for a low-interest loan, has no staff left in dozens of counties across the country, forcing farmers to travel long distances for assistance or to simply give up. Among divisions that directly work with farmers and aid rural residents, the percentage of departures is even higher.

The Agriculture Department said that it currently had about 93,000 employees after hiring more workers this year, and that it believed staffing levels were adequate as “services and supports have become more targeted and efficient” through planned technological improvements.

Still, its plans to fundamentally overhaul the agency, as well as funding cuts proposed by President Trump’s latest budget, are likely to deepen difficulties for farmers and rural communities.

Already, the agency is moving more than half of its staff in the Washington region out of the nation’s capital, a move that is all but certain to further thin the ranks of the agency. Such losses will affect the department’s ability to finance home loans, carry out agricultural research and service farmers, according to federal workers, farm groups and rural lenders. (Unions and farm organizations have mounted a legal challenge to that plan.)

Likewise, Mr. Trump’s budget for the next fiscal year proposes a nearly $5 billion cut to the Agriculture Department, essentially eliminating programs for beginning farmers, conservation and rural aid.

Some of the steepest cuts have fallen on a part of the Agriculture Department responsible for improving the economy and infrastructure in rural communities, leading to long delays in aid for residents and charities alike.

The subagency, known as Rural Development, has lost about 1,700 workers, or more than a third of its staff, since the Trump administration took office.

In New Mexico, questions directed at the agency often languish for weeks, as do approvals of key documents, with emails and queries bouncing among staff members scattered across the state and in Washington, said Lorenzo Alba Jr., the executive director of Casa de Peregrinos, an anti-hunger charity in the area.

After receiving a grant from the Rural Development section at the end of the Biden administration to build a food pantry in Hatch, N.M., the charity is still waiting for $300,000 in federal funding. For now, Casa de Peregrinos has cobbled together other sources of financing to set up and operate a makeshift pantry with limited hours and food varieties, despite no refrigeration or air conditioning.

“Our pantry should have been up and running, fully renovated by now,” Mr. Alba said. He added that the delays had led costs to balloon to $600,000 from $475,000, money the charity could have used to buy more food and serve more families.

“I quit blaming the U.S.D.A. on this because I didn’t know what they were going through,” he said. “Now I do.”

It is unclear whether staffing cuts have been a factor, but in the last year the subagency has also financed far fewer loans and grants. As of mid-August, with a little over a month left in the 2026 fiscal year, the agency has approved nearly 52,000 investments worth $15.8 billion. In comparison, in the past three fiscal years, the agency made between 63,000 and 74,000 investments totaling $24 billion to $40 billion annually.

Another crucial service the department offers — helping producers carry out sustainable farming practices through its Natural Resources Conservation Service — has lost more than 2,700 workers, or nearly a fourth of its staff, forcing farmers to miss contract deadlines and turn to expensive private consultants for advice.

In central Nebraska, Clay Govier, who farms corn and soybeans on 3,500 acres in Broken Bow, described the cascading effect of 50 percent staffing cuts at his local conservation agency. The technician he had worked with took a buyout at the start of the Trump administration. Now, Mr. Govier and his family coordinate with someone who travels between two counties to survey different farms.

Though the technician is knowledgeable, “he’s stretched very thin because if he needs a signature, he has to drive to our farm and then he drives back or we have to drive to him, and it just burns up an entire morning to get some basic paperwork done,” Mr. Govier said.

As a result, the office is missing more details and overlooking crucial steps to verifying the farmers’ practices these days, leading to delays in the contract cycle and payments.

“Farming is an art and a science,” he said. “It’s so different for every operation, every state, every region, so you need local N.R.C.S. staff that understand their region and how to implement these programs.”

In southwestern Pennsylvania, Amanda Butterfield worked with the conservation service for nearly a decade, first to restore roughly 180 acres of strip-mined land in Meyersdale into pasture for a herd of beef cattle. After her technician shared anecdotes about burnout and long working hours, Ms. Butterfield turned instead to private consultants who work for agribusinesses. But that advice often comes at a steeper cost, like the expectation of buying certain products.

Ms. Butterfield also added that staffing turnover at her local Farm Service Agency had led to errors and inefficiencies: A new worker hired to replace an employee who had left asked her husband to report crop acreage, unaware that the ranch did not grow crops at all.

“We’ve completely lost a whole group of experts within our communities across the United States that can no longer help and support us,” she said.

item.title: Firefighters Grapple With Nevada Blaze That Drove Thousands From Homes
item.description:
Firefighters on Monday were still trying to tame a wildfire northwest of Reno, Nev., that has driven tens of thousands of people from their homes and that is keeping many more ready to run from the flames.

The blaze, known as the Hawk fire, has burned more than 15,000 acres since it began Saturday in the Sierra Nevada foothills. Firefighters had contained 27 percent of the fire, officials said at a community meeting on Monday night.

Officials said that seven people had been injured, including three firefighters, and that 32 homes had been destroyed and six others damaged.

About 23,000 people had been ordered to evacuate, and an additional 40,000 had been warned that they might need to leave at a moment’s notice.

By Monday night, evacuation orders had been downgraded to warnings in some areas and the number of displaced residents had fallen to about 14,900 after some were allowed to return home, said Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District Chief Richard Edwards. He added that officials had reopened sections of U.S. Route 395, along the fire’s northern edge.

Throughout Monday, power had been restored to about 3,000 households, leaving 6,000 still without electricity and 250 without gas, said Scott Kaufmann, NV Energy’s vice president for transmission, at the community meeting.

Mayor Hillary Schieve of Reno urged people to return to their homes only after they received an all-clear, in order to prevent further strain on emergency agencies and to lessen risks for rescuers.

“We end up putting others’ lives at risk, because they got to go in and help you,” she said. “So when we ask you to do it, we’re also asking you to help save other lives.”

Some people had also illegally flown drones over the fire, posing a risk to firefighters and ground crews, and tried to hike in freshly burned areas, the authorities said.

Marcus Butler, 30, a Lemmon Valley resident, evacuated his home Saturday and stayed for two nights at a Hampton Inn in Sparks, adjacent to Reno.

On Monday morning, he showed up to the Reno-Sparks Convention Center, which is serving as an evacuation shelter, to see if he could stay in his car in the parking lot. He hadn’t seen smoke in the sky, but his home remained in a no-go zone. “Maybe the fire’s hidden and we can’t see it,” he said.

On Sunday evening, firefighters had expected the blaze to reach “pockets of dense fuels” as it advanced toward Reno, a city of almost 300,000 near the border of Nevada and California.

But on Monday, local officials expressed optimism in their efforts to handle the fire, particularly at the southern end of the blaze, where firefighters largely stopped it from advancing.

“Fire behavior was less extreme than anticipated in some areas, allowing crews to hold established lines and reposition resources to reinforce suppression efforts,” city officials said in a morning update.

Fire perimeters

Source: National Interagency Fire Center. The New York Times

Extreme heat, dry conditions and strong winds have helped the Hawk fire expand. It is the second large blaze in the area in the past three weeks.

Arid conditions have propelled an active wildfire season across the American West this summer. In Washington State, hundreds of homes and more than 400,000 acres burned. In Oregon, a record 2.4 million acres have burned in 2026, according to state authorities.

Mr. Butler is wrapping up his job as a summer camp manager in Portola, Calif., and is set to move home to New England. “More floods, but no more wildfires,” he said. “I know it’s flooding out there, but I’d rather take the floods instead of the fires.”

In Nevada, hot and dry conditions, fuel and mountainous terrain will complicate efforts to suppress the flames. Winds were expected to pick up Monday afternoon.

The fire’s western portion remained a challenge, and firefighters were working to keep the blaze out of flatter terrain. City officials said on Monday night that most of the contained area was along the fire’s south end, where some residents had been allowed to return.

Officials said that the fire was caused by a person but that it was not yet clear whether it had been intentional.

More than 800 personnel, as well as canine search teams, are assisting with the effort to stop the blaze, including firefighters from at least 15 other states, Australia and New Zealand. The National Guard and the local police are also helping safeguard neighborhoods.

Barry and Karen Lewis had been eyeing the Hawk fire’s smoke since midday Saturday as they prepared to evacuate from their Lemmon Valley home. When they got evacuation alerts, they quickly left in their R.V.

The husband and wife have lived there since 2010 and said they had assumed that being in a desert area meant fewer wildfire risks.

“All the movies, you see the fires in the forest,” said Mr. Lewis, 72.

Judson Jones, Livia Albeck-Ripka and Francesca Regalado contributed reporting.

item.title: College Applications Are Changing Again, Thanks to A.I. and Politics
item.description:
A new era of college admissions is unfolding after years of turmoil.

Standardized testing requirements are being revived, or are under consideration, from coast to coast. Admissions officers at both big public schools, like the University of Georgia, and top-tier private institutions, like Washington University in St. Louis, are shedding some application essays. Administrators everywhere are fretting about what role artificial intelligence may play in applications.

The Covid pandemic led many schools to loosen their processes and, in many cases, rely more on components like essays. But A.I.’s rise, questions about student preparation, the end of affirmative action and the Trump administration’s campaign to prioritize “merit” in admissions are driving a swing back.

College applications were up during the last admissions cycle, after a more diverse pool of students applied and students applied to more schools on average. But demographic shifts are expected to send enrollments diving in the coming years. At the same time, higher education is wrestling with public mistrust and concerns about the value of college, especially as A.I. starts to reshape the work force.

As schools prepare for a future with fewer students and more A.I., approaches that make applying to college simpler — and more attractive to families — could help them cushion the impact.

The personal essay is still central to many college applications. But supplementary essays are falling out of favor.

Tulane University, for instance, paused its requirement for applicants to write about why they want to attend the school. Concerns about potential A.I.-generated essays “were definitely a factor” in the decision, said Michael Strecker, a university spokesman.

Some admissions officers said they don’t use A.I. detection systems, which are not always accurate.

Georgia, Cornell University, the University of Virginia and Texas Christian University have recently pared back essay requirements. Washington University dropped an optional essay that many applicants apparently did not consider truly optional.

Reducing the number of required essays makes applying easier, which tends to raise a school’s application numbers. By attracting more applicants, a school lowers its acceptance rate, which can make it appear more exclusive — though many colleges do not want to be seen as intentionally pumping up rejection notices.

Mr. Strecker, the Tulane spokesman, said by email that “reducing our admit rate to appear more selective was, in no way, a reason” for pausing a supplemental essay. The “Why Tulane?” essay had just not factored heavily into the school’s selection decisions in recent years, he said.

Tulane still requires that applicants write a personal essay, and the school makes admission decisions largely based on “applicants’ academic record, testing profile, impact and involvement outside the classroom, letters of recommendation” and the personal essay, Mr. Strecker said.

David Graves, executive director of undergraduate admissions at Georgia, said he figures “every admissions office has concerns about essays being written by A.I.” While Georgia’s decision to drop a supplemental essay was more about simplifying the process for applicants, other experts said the possibility that students are using A.I. to help with essays is a rising concern.

“A.I. has hastened the realization that the written word in this context isn’t necessarily an accurate representation of how somebody thinks and how somebody writes,” said Christoph Guttentag, who retired in 2025 as dean of undergraduate admissions at Duke University after having read student applications for 42 years.

The University of Pennsylvania has lately tried to tell applicants what they can — and cannot do — with A.I. Talking through an idea with a parent or teacher or asking that person to proofread is fine. So is using A.I. to sort through ideas or double-check grammar, the university says.

But Penn, which acknowledges using A.I. for administrative but not evaluative purposes in admissions, also tells applicants if “you couldn’t explain, in an interview or conversation, how you arrived at what you wrote, or speak to it in your own words, it isn’t ready to submit.”

In St. Louis, where Washington University has long worked to carve out a spot among the nation’s most respected schools, officials some years ago added an “optional” essay for students to showcase more of themselves, said Ronné Turner, vice provost for enrollment management. The school is now phasing it out after deciding much of the information students shared was redundant.

The team also heard from high school guidance counselors that students often believed that skipping the essay would reflect poorly on them.

The school will still require a personal essay and another on what the student might want to study.

“We’re asking them just for the information we need to make good admission decisions,” she said.

What data universities need remains a significant flashpoint. The 2023 Supreme Court decision striking down race-conscious admissions programs lurks in many internal deliberations about requirements and processes. In that ruling, Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. wrote that an applicant “must be treated based on his or her experiences as an individual — not on the basis of race.”

He also said that the court’s opinion should not be “construed as prohibiting universities from considering an applicant’s discussion of how race affected his or her life, be it through discrimination, inspiration or otherwise.”

The Trump administration has argued that the court’s opinion should be interpreted to banish any consideration of race in admissions. Many university leaders and lawyers privately contest the White House’s view, but a series of Justice Department inquiries into admissions practices across the country has left them unnerved and searching for ways to avoid scrutiny.

Many figures inside the Trump administration want schools to rely on measures they see as more merit-based, like test scores and grades. For a variety of reasons, many schools that relaxed their testing mandates during the pandemic are bringing them back. In June, for instance, Columbia University became the last Ivy League institution to announce plans to once again require scores from prospective undergraduate students.

The testing debate is erupting anew in the nation’s most populous state, where the 10-campus University of California system is considering a resurrection of its standardized testing mandate. Given the public system’s prestige and size — it has about 238,000 undergraduate students — a change could reverberate across the national landscape.

The system has drawn plenty of skepticism from the Trump administration, but much of the agitation is coming from faculty members, who say that fewer students appeared ready for U.C.’s rigors after the system moved in 2020 to do away with standardized testing.

“Starting around 2022, 2023, I noticed that students were struggling to complete even the homework assignments — the same assignments that I’ve been giving for 15 years,” Pradeep Sen, an engineering professor at the University of California, Santa Barbara, told regents in July. “This means I need to spend class time teaching students stuff they’re supposed to know already, which is really impacting the ability to cover the stuff that I need to cover.”

Dr. Sen said he was sensitive to the possibility that students of various demographics might perform differently than others on standardized tests. “The answer,” he said during the regents’ meeting, “is not to get rid of the one metric that ensures students have a proper foundation to succeed in college.”

In the same meeting, Jessie Ryan, the president of the California-based Campaign for College Opportunity, warned that reinstating the SAT was “absolutely the wrong solution to an undefined problem.”

Retention and graduation rates had stayed stable or increased since the university system eliminated standardized tests, she said.

“If, in fact, we want to address college preparation, we should be looking not at becoming more selective, but being more supportive to students,” she said.

Maria Anguiano, the chair of the Board of Regents, said that public debates about college readiness had focused “too narrowly” on admissions and standardized testing. Ms. Anguiano said the university’s academic senate would conduct a review of standardized testing, among other topics, and submit a recommendation by the end of the academic year.

The college admissions process has been a rollercoaster for seemingly time immemorial. But it's been especially up-and-down the last few years as schools have reeled from the pandemic, considered the fairness (or unfairness) of standardized testing and faced a lot more mistrust. So now the admissions landscape is shifting again, with some of the biggest changes unfolding at major public universities and elite schools.

item.title: Ex-Illinois Deputy Who Murdered Black Woman Dies in Prison
item.description:
A former Illinois sheriff’s deputy who shot and killed a Black woman at her home after she called 911 died on Sunday while serving a 20-year murder sentence.

Sean Grayson, 32, who was white, was found guilty in October of second-degree murder in the 2024 killing of Sonya Massey, a rare instance of an American law enforcement officer convicted of a crime in an on-duty shooting.

He was sentenced in January and had been in prison for just over six months when he died.

His lawyer, Daniel Fultz, confirmed his death but declined to provide any further details.

Mr. Grayson had applied for medical release but was unanimously denied by the Illinois Prisoner Review Board last month. The Illinois Department of Corrections did not immediately return a request for information.

During his sentencing, Mr. Grayson’s lawyers said he had colon cancer that had spread to his liver and lungs, and they urged Judge Ryan Cadagin for leniency. Judge Cadagin instead gave Mr. Grayson the maximum sentence allowed.

Ms. Massey, who was 36, had called 911 for help in July 2024 because she was worried someone was lurking outside her house near Springfield, Ill.

Mr. Grayson and another deputy responded to the call, and after looking through the yard, found no one hiding. They then knocked on Ms. Massey’s front door, spoke with her and stepped inside.

The conversation was amiable until Ms. Massey moved to remove a pot of hot water from her stove. After picking up the pot, she said, “I rebuke you in the name of Jesus.”

The encounter quickly escalated, and Mr. Grayson told Ms. Massey to drop the pot, threatening to shoot her in the face if she did not. Within seconds, the deputies had pulled their guns, and Mr. Grayson fatally shot Ms. Massey in the head.

Illinois State Police released body camera footage of the exchange.

The day before the shooting, Ms. Massey’s mother had called 911 and told the dispatcher that her daughter was having mental health issues.

Mr. Grayson told the jury in October that he had feared for his safety when Ms. Massey lifted the pot of hot water, and that the only tool he had to stop the threat was his weapon. Prosecutors argued that he had needlessly escalated the situation.

The Sangamon County Sheriff’s Office fired Mr. Grayson shortly after the shooting. The other deputy in the encounter, who had tried to stop Ms. Massey’s bleeding after she was shot, was not charged.

The Justice Department later opened an investigation, telling officials in Sangamon County that the shooting raised “serious concerns” about the way the sheriff’s office interacted with Black people and people with behavioral health disabilities.

In January, the agency said it had found no discriminatory practices behind the fatal shooting.

item.title: Trump Lays It on the Line for Darline Graham
item.description:
President Trump has stuck his neck out for Senator Darline Graham.

In the weeks leading up to South Carolina’s primary election runoff for Senate on Tuesday, Mr. Trump traveled to Myrtle Beach to rally supporters and personally called high-level state officials to compel them to endorse Ms. Graham. A super PAC run by his advisers, MAGA Inc., notoriously wary to spend on races this cycle, invested more than $800,000 on phone calls on her behalf, according to campaign finance filings released on Monday, nearly a third of the total the committee has spent this year.

On the line: The president’s credibility in a state that twice in the last six months has rejected his preferences. In June, voters discarded his first choice for governor, prompting him to make a second endorsement in the final stretch. And earlier this year, the Republican-held State Senate declined to take up a new congressional map backed by Mr. Trump and other national Republicans that would have eliminated South Carolina’s lone majority Black district, which is held by a Democrat.

With several high-profile losses in other states, Mr. Trump’s national endorsement track record is at stake, too. Because he touted Ms. Graham more enthusiastically than most other candidates, a loss for her would amount to a huge loss for him.

“What I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot,” Mr. Trump said at the rally in Myrtle Beach on Friday. “Just come and vote. It’s so important.”

Ms. Graham is facing Representative Ralph Norman, a hard-line conservative who has occasionally irked the president, in the race to serve a full, six-year term following the death of Senator Lindsey Graham in July. The winner in the solidly Republican state will compete in November against Dr. Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee.

A longtime administrator of disability services, Ms. Graham had never held public office until the state’s governor appointed her to serve out the remainder of her brother’s term in the Senate. Weeks later, on Aug. 11, she finished first in a crowded special primary election, boosted by Mr. Trump’s endorsement and a pitch to voters that she would carry on the most popular parts of her brother’s tenure. That included pledges to keep his staff, who are well-liked for their constituent services, and to follow the wishes of the president. But in the final week of a whirlwind election the political winds have shifted against her.

Last week, during the only televised debate of the runoff, Ms. Graham stumbled over a question about the importance of Taiwan to U.S. interests, admitting that she was “not that informed on national security.” A day earlier, the Republican Party chapter in her home county endorsed Mr. Norman. Plenty of empty space was visible at Mr. Trump’s rally in Myrtle Beach on Friday, and not everyone who attended seemed entirely sold on Ms. Graham.

Some attendees said they were there to learn more about her. Most had heard her comment about not knowing enough about foreign policy and offered tepid defenses of her ignorance, saying she could learn on the job.

“You know, she’s never done it before, but she knows politics well,” Mr. Trump said of Ms. Graham at the rally on Friday. “But she loves our military; she loves things that have to do with greatness for America.”

Other voters across the state over the last week expressed skepticism in interviews over what they described as a feeling that political insiders in Washington, including the president, were trying to choose their senator for them.

“This is just inside establishment B.S.,” said Curtis Loftis, the state treasurer who endorsed Mr. Norman, of Ms. Graham’s candidacy. “She’s been asked by the president and then asked by the governor, and this has all just been foisted on her.”Neither Ms. Graham’s campaign nor MAGA Inc. responded to requests for comments on the state of the race.

Brittany Yanick, a spokeswoman for Mr. Norman, said in a statement that the campaign is “feeling great” headed into Election Day.

The campaigns of Ms. Graham and Mr. Norman, along with officials with MAGA Inc., did not immediately respond to requests for comments on the state of the race.

South Carolina has a long history of bristling at top-down politics. In 2018, Henry McMaster, the lieutenant governor at the time, was forced into a runoff election for governor against a 39-year-old political newcomer, despite having the support of Mr. Trump.

Ms. Graham, in part with the help of Mr. Trump, has racked up endorsements from some of South Carolina’s most powerful officials. Senator Tim Scott, who chairs the Senate Republicans’ campaign arm, has been a fierce advocate. Representative Russell Fry, one of her chief opponents in the primary election in July, backed her after the president asked him to. And Mr. McMaster, who initially refrained from weighing in on the primary, endorsed Ms. Graham the day Mr. Trump touched down in his state for the rally.

The president had called Mr. McMaster earlier that week, two people familiar with the conversation said.

He had also called Mark Sanford, a former South Carolina governor and congressman who has been openly critical of the president, to urge him to endorse Ms. Graham. On the day of Mr. Trump’s visit to the state, Mr. Sanford endorsed Mr. Norman, saying in a lengthy statement that “as much as I would like to honor tradition and old friendships, the stakes are simply too high as our nation really is at a financial tipping point.”

On the trail, Mr. Norman frequently touts his endorsements from Senators Rick Scott of Florida and Mike Lee of Utah, two Republicans who have drawn accolades from the party’s conservative base because they are frequently a thorn in the side of their party’s leadership.

Rob Godfrey, a longtime South Carolina Republican political strategist, said primary voters in the state are typically highly informed and eager to make their own decisions at the ballot box.

“Our voters don’t always take advice from other politicians, no matter what office they hold, about who to support,” he said. “While both of these candidates have their fair share of endorsements, our voters are hyper-informed, thanks to the number of candidates they meet face-to-face, take their own agency seriously at the ballot box, have an independent streak and expect they’ll know the person they end up supporting personally.”

Over the weekend, the candidates stopped by local restaurants and held town halls, looking to personally greet as many South Carolinians as possible. But on Monday night, hours before Election Day, Ms. Graham will do something that her opponent cannot: participate in a virtual rally with one of her fiercest supporters, Mr. Trump.

Shawn McCreesh and Theodore Schleifer contributed reporting.

item.title: U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln Sailor Says Father Was Arrested by Border Patrol
item.description:
A Navy sailor, on his way home after a long deployment aboard the aircraft carrier U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln in support of the war with Iran, said his father had been detained by immigration authorities in the United States.

“I’ve been deployed for over nine months, out at sea in the Middle East aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, fighting for a country that has given me everything,” the sailor, Joshua Aviles, wrote on Facebook on Saturday. He said his father, Luis Manuel Aviles, 48, had a driver’s license, Social Security card and a permit to work in the United States.

“We have done everything through immigration to get his green card approved, and we are just waiting,” Mr. Aviles wrote.

The post has generated widespread attention, partly because of recent reports about poor conditions aboard the carrier caused by supply challenges following Iran’s destruction of a U.S. Navy base in Bahrain. On Thursday, the beleaguered carrier, deployed in support of the war in Iran, started its journey home to San Diego, a voyage of about 13,000 miles.

“This is heartbreaking for me,” Mr. Aviles added. “I don’t know how I can mentally continue working 12+ hour days knowing that my dad is somewhere, possibly being treated like a criminal. My dad’s only ‘crime’ was coming to this country to give my siblings and me a better life.”

The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement on Monday that Border Patrol officers arrested Luis Manuel Aviles Roa on Saturday during a vehicle stop in Key West, Fla. The statement said the agency did not know when or where he had entered the United States, but said that he was in the country illegally.

“He will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings,” the statement said.

In his Facebook post, Joshua Aviles said he was notified on Saturday that his father had been taken into custody. “Dad, I don’t know where you are right now, but know that I am doing everything I can to bring you back home,” he wrote. “I love you with all my heart. Please stay strong. I’m coming home, Dad.”

The sailor’s mother, Argelia Aviles, told The Associated Press that Joshua’s father, a handyman, was arrested after leaving his house to take his car to the mechanic. He has lived in the United States for 19 years, The A.P. reported.

The Homeland Security Department’s statement said that military service by an immediate relative “does not automatically grant parole, lawful status, or immunity from immigration enforcement.”

A government program called Parole in Place has served as a recruiting tool for the military; it shields undocumented parents and spouses of service members from deportation and providing an expedited pathway to permanent residency. Service members must apply to be included in the program.

Democratic lawmakers this month expressed concerns about the extended deployment of the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln after reports about poor living conditions and a lack of downtime for its crew of about 5,000 sailors.

Adm. Brad Cooper, who heads U.S. Central Command, said in an opinion essay published in The Wall Street Journal on Aug. 16 that many of the issues were “old news.” He has also acknowledged the difficulty of the long deployment.

President Trump’s second term has been defined by a crackdown on undocumented immigrants. An A.P. investigation this month said more than 50 parents and spouses of active-duty service members had been detained during Mr. Trump’s second term. At least six have been deported and one self-deported, it reported.

Earlier this year, an immigration judge terminated a deportation case against an undocumented father of three U.S. Marines.

item.title: The Local: Walkie-talkies for grief
item.description:
Good afternoon. It has been nearly a year since the shooting at Annunciation Catholic School that killed two children, injured dozens and shook the Twin Cities. Our colleague Talya Minsberg has the story of how trauma therapists helped the community recover. It’s about hope amid profound grief.

We also have some lighter material, including a special Minnesota-themed Midi crossword. See how many Gopher State connections you can spot. First, here are a few of the top local stories we’re following.

The federal government’s purchase of a former prison in the small city of Appleton might seem like an economic boon. Madison McVan of Minnesota Reformer explains how it could turn out to be the opposite.

Keith Ellison, Minnesota’s attorney general, and Ron Schutz, the Republican trying to unseat him, are leaning on entirely different issues. The Minnesota Star Tribune shows the campaign split-screen.

In a goof gone horrifically wrong, a man working to clear branches in Apple Valley was killed on Thursday when a grapple apparently closed on his head, FOX 9 reports.

Sign up here to get this newsletter delivered to your inbox or share this link with a friend who might like to join us.

By Talya Minsberg

After the shooting that killed 8-year-old Fletcher Merkel and 10-year-old Harper Moyski during a back-to-school Mass, the Annunciation community faced a process that has become all too common. Unthinkable grief, a barrage of media attention, trauma and recovery services, and eventually, an impossibly difficult question: How do you go back to school?

At Annunciation, the answer came in the shape of a butterfly, with the help of walkie-talkies.

A group of clinicians from the Washburn Center for Children, a mental health organization, embedded with the school to provide counseling and support when the students returned to the classroom. The organization, which has served Minnesota since 1883, began with triage services and expanded into a network of warm, trusted helpers who are on call via walkie-talkie.

They are always available on Channel 2. Their logo, a butterfly, has become a symbol of support. When a student needed a break, the child could make a peace sign or ask a teacher, “Can I have a Washburn friend?”

The trauma therapists at the school, called butterflies by some or simply the Helpers, will be back when classes start up again next week.

Dr. David Schonfeld, the director of the National Center for School Crisis and Bereavement, said this kind of continuing local partnership was highly atypical.

The children have found a sense of comfort in the Helpers’ continuing presence, said Jenny Britton, the chief clinical officer at Washburn.

“They could look at each other and say, ‘You know, we’ve all been through this together,’” she said. “‘If I cry, or I’m having a hard day, or I need to take a break, I’m not judged here for that.’”

More on Annunciation:

Watch: The Star Tribune had four families keep video diaries over the past year. What they captured is beautiful, gut-wrenching and, at times, deeply hopeful. Six months in, Sara Slack, a first-grade teacher, said, “The main thing that comes to mind for me is wanting our story to remain relevant.”

Read: I’ll never forget watching Matt DeBoer, the principal of Annunciation, speak hours after the shooting. Later, he said, “It’s not what I signed up for, but it’s what I’m called to do.” Learn more about DeBoer in this breathtaking profile from The Strib.

Listen: Harper’s mother, Jackie Flavin, and best friend, Orla McGarvey, remembered her during a conversation for StoryCorps. “We can talk to each other whenever we’re sad and stuff,” Orla said.

Our colleague Ian Livengood on the Games team has created a special Minnesota-themed puzzle to celebrate our state as The Local kicks off. The Midi is a daily midsize crossword puzzle, bigger than the Mini but a quicker solve than the full Crossword.

You’ll find Minnesota-themed clues and answers throughout today’s Midi. The puzzle is titled “Things Are Looking Up,” and we couldn’t agree more.

Top Times stories, selected for Minnesota readers. We have made these links free for readers of The Local.

CBD for dogs: Even before Minnesota legalized marijuana, CBD products were popular. Now they’re being marketed for dogs, but are they actually good for them?

Canada tariffs: President Trump threatened even higher tariffs today on Minnesota’s largest international trading partner after talks broke down this weekend.

E. coli and salmonella: A Minnesota company’s alfalfa sprouts have been linked to dozens of cases of E. coli and salmonella in 15 states.

A.I.: In Minnesota and across the country, data centers have become the “epicenter of the midterm elections.”

Cheaper drugs: Illicit drugs have gotten stronger and less expensive since the 1980s. Minnesota recently tightened rules on kratom, an opioid-like drug that is still legal here.

We’re 38 days away from the start of the Minnesota Wild season, but that doesn’t mean it’s too soon to make predictions.

More than 4,600 readers responded to The Athletic’s annual Wild survey with sighs and cautious optimism. Overall, fans still believe wholeheartedly in Bill Guerin, the general manager of the team. That’s despite how last season ended — what The Athletic called “the most shocking loss in Minnesota Wild playoff history.”

Michael Russo, who covers the N.H.L. for The Athletic, attributes some of the optimism to Quinn Hughes, the defenseman who was traded to the team in 2025.

“Trading for Hughes was the kind of franchise-altering move fans love and reinforced the idea Guerin will swing for the fences,” he wrote, “and Hughes validated the confidence in his play in Minnesota and at the Olympics.”

Read how Wild fans feel about New Jersey Devils fans, what the value of a Hughes extension is and who should play with Kirill Kaprizov.

— Talya Minsberg

Today’s uneventful forecast may be the quiet before. Tuesday is expected to bring thunderstorms, strong winds and hail that could stretch into Wednesday morning.

Every year, thousands of Minnesota artists learn that their work won’t be among those selected for display at the State Fair’s Juried Fine Art Show. But all is not lost.

For the third year running, the Douglas Flanders & Associates gallery in Minneapolis will host a “Reject Show.”

It opens on Saturday. Syril McNally, the gallery’s director, said the idea of a reject show — or salon des refusés — originated in France in the late 1800s when Impressionist painters were turned away from museums and top galleries.

It has become so popular that some artists even want the fair to reject them so they’re eligible to show their work here, writes The Star Tribune’s art critic and reporter Alicia Eler.

item.title: Judge Orders U.S. to Return Deported Man at Risk of Torture
item.description:
A federal judge ordered the Trump administration to immediately bring back a Mexican man who was deported this month despite proving to an immigration court that he would likely face torture in Mexico.

The man, who is in his late 40s and was referred to in court documents only as John Doe, helped U.S. authorities by testifying against Mexican drug cartels.

The man provided information to U.S. law enforcement that put his and his family members’ lives at “significant risk,” according to the order, which was issued by Judge Stephanie Gallagher in Maryland on Friday. The court found that the administration’s revocation of protections barring his removal “likely violated his procedural due process rights,” exceeding the government’s lawful authority.

The head of Immigration and Customs Enforcement moved to reverse his protections after the State Department received diplomatic assurances from the Mexican government that the man would not be harmed, according to background information on the case included in the judge’s order.

The ruling was the latest legal blow to President Trump’s mass deportation campaign at a time when administration officials are facing pressure from his base to accelerate removals.

The New York Times reported this month that the department used a rare authority this summer to deport a group of Mexican nationals whose removal had been blocked over concerns they would be tortured if returned to their home country, citing diplomatic assurances from the Mexican government that the deportees would not be harmed if returned.

But in her ruling, Judge Gallagher said there was an “immense public interest in ensuring that persons who risk their personal safety to assist the government in prosecuting wrongdoing are not placed in harm’s way by the very entity they assisted.”

The Department of Homeland Security and the Mexican government did not respond to requests for comment.

Anna Tijerina, an immigration attorney representing the man, said on Monday that he had not yet been returned to the United States, and the process could take several weeks.

“His life is at risk in Mexico, and deporting somebody without a meaningful opportunity to learn about those diplomatic assurances or challenge the termination goes against his rights,” Ms. Tijerina said.

The judge’s order detailed the repeated efforts administration officials took to try to deport the man, who they tried to remove several times over the span of a month.

An immigration judge had granted the man a “deferral of removal” under the Convention Against Torture two years ago. He was living in Maryland until he was detained at a routine check-in with ICE in January.

He spent six months in a detention facility in Louisiana before federal authorities sent him to Guatemala on July 10, according to the order. But Guatemalan officials rejected him and took him to a Mexican consular officer in Guatemala to return him to his home country.

But after learning about his protection, the consular officer informed the man that he would be returned to the United States instead.

About five days later, the U.S. government allegedly removed him directly to Mexico but officials there refused to accept him. He was then returned to the United States, the order said.

Then, on July 21, the Trump administration “purportedly” served him with a termination notice of his deferral of removal after the State Department received diplomatic assurances from the Mexican government that he would not be tortured if returned to the country, according to the order. Ms. Tijerina, his attorney, said he does not have any recollection of receiving the termination notice.

The acting head of ICE, David Venturella, and the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, had “consulted and determined that these assurances were reliable,” the order said.

It was an unusual move by the federal government. Typically, officials seeking to strip someone of their deportation protections ask an immigration judge, which allows the immigrant to argue in favor of staying.

On Aug. 1, the federal government deported the man to Mexico, where he has remained in hiding out of fear that the “cartels that he provided information against will find him and torture or kill him before he can return to the United States,” according to the order. The man was sent to a region of Mexico where there is “active cartel activity” without his money or belongings. He has been relying on the help of strangers while attempting to stay in hiding, the order said.

The judge also said that if the man is detained, he must remain within 200 miles of the court in Baltimore and have reasonable access to his attorneys.

The decision followed a string of cases in which federal judges have ordered the Trump administration to return people who were wrongly deported.

Last year, the Salvadoran immigrant Kilmar Armando Abrego Garcia was wrongfully expelled from Maryland, despite an immigration judge’s earlier ruling that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced a credible fear of persecution. Although he has since been returned to the United States, the administration has said it wants to send him to Liberia. His attorneys are fighting that effort in court.

In March, a federal judge ordered the U.S. government to bring back a California woman who had been living in the country for more than 27 years and had been deported to Mexico, despite having protections through the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, known as DACA.

And about two months later, another federal judge ruled that the Trump administration had most likely violated the law by deporting a Colombian woman to the Democratic Republic of Congo, despite that country’s refusal to take her.

item.title: A Suspect Was Outrunning the Police. So the Officers Jumped in an Uber.
item.description:
Anthony Baines, an Uber driver in Houston, was at a stop sign, on his way to pick up a rider this month when he saw a man with no shirt and no shoes sprinting by. Two police officers were chasing the man.

Then one of the officers ran up to Mr. Baines’s car and jumped in the front seat.

“That way! Go, go, go, go!” she said, commanding him to follow the man, who had just been accused of threatening to shoot a woman and her two children.

“And the next thing I know, we’re chasing the guy,” Mr. Baines said in an interview on Monday.

Over the next three minutes, Mr. Baines found himself the unlikely driver in a late-night police pursuit. First, he stopped to pick up the officer’s partner, who jumped in the back seat. Then he drove around, following the officers’ directions as they searched for the man on the dark streets of the Heights, a residential neighborhood in northwest Houston.

The short, bizarre chase shortly after midnight on Aug. 8 was captured on video by a camera in Mr. Baines’s Nissan Pathfinder.

“Which way did he go?” one of the officers asks in the footage, as their police radios crackle over the sounds of Mr. Baines’s jazz playlist. “Over there,” the other officer says.

“I was absolutely shocked to be in that situation,” Mr. Baines said in the interview. “This is one of those things you see in a movie — the police pursuing the criminal and get in some dude’s car and tell him to go.”

Erika Ramirez, a spokeswoman for the Houston Police Department, said the officers were responding to a report that a man had threatened to shoot a woman and her two children during a dispute. The man believed someone had stolen his property, and he and the woman had “exchanged words” at an apartment building, Ms. Ramirez said.

When the officers tried to detain the man, he managed to pull away from them, prompting them to chase him on foot, Ms. Ramirez said.

“While trying to locate him, a nearby citizen assisted the officers by giving them a ride,” Ms. Ramirez said. “The citizen then dropped the officers back at the apartment where they used patrol vehicles to continue searching for the suspect.”

Ms. Ramirez said on Monday that the police had not located the unidentified man. As for Mr. Baines, she said, “We’re thankful for him helping us.”

The video from Mr. Baines’s camera shows him watching the first officer chase the man down the street. When the second officer runs up to Mr. Baines’s Nissan at the stop sign, she says, “Hey! Give me a ride over there! Please,” and he says, “All right,” and lets her in.

“Go! Drive that way!” she says.

Mr. Baines, 39, said he was running on adrenaline during the low-speed pursuit, which was previously reported by KPRC, a Houston news station.

He has driven for Uber for about two years, usually on weekend nights before and after bars close, he said. Before that, he served for eight years in the Army and did a tour in Iraq as an Apache helicopter mechanic.

“That was really the only way I was able to keep my composure,” Mr. Baines said of his military experience. “But I don’t approach Uber driving that way so it did catch me off guard.”

Rachel Harmon, director of the Center for Criminal Justice at the University of Virginia School of Law, said the chase was “definitely unusual” and raised questions about when the police should ask for the public’s help.

“You could imagine circumstances when police officers need to get from Point A to Point B, and it doesn’t increase the risk to ask members of the public for help in doing so,” she said.

But police pursuits have led to crashes, some of them fatal, over the years, Professor Harmon noted. “Uber drivers aren’t trained to engage in pursuits,” she added.

Kirk D. Burkhalter, a retired New York City police detective and law professor at New York Law School, said the police generally avoid asking civilians for help in pursuits and other situations that could put them in danger. But he said was impressed with the way Mr. Baines handled the situation.

“Kudos to the Uber driver. He did all those things safely,” Professor Burkhalter said. “He kept his head and followed those commands.”

Uber did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Baines said wife reminded him later that he could have been in danger if he and the officers had located the suspect. But he said he was glad he had been part of the operation.

“It was a privilege to help,” Mr. Baines said. “I would definitely do it again.”

After dropping off the officers, Mr. Baines said, he picked up the customer who had summoned him for a ride earlier.

“I apologized for the inconvenience and said, ‘I just had the one of the craziest experiences of my life,’” Mr. Baines said. “I got him to his destination and he gave me five stars.”

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: Court Allows Trump to Pursue Mail Voting Limits, for Now
item.description:
A divided Supreme Court on Monday allowed the Trump administration to move forward with plans to restrict mail-in voting before the midterm elections.

In an emergency opinion, the justices said President Trump could proceed with implementing an executive order he had signed, which directed the U.S. Postal Service to help decide which voters should receive mail-in ballots. Under the executive order, the Department of Homeland Security will also create lists of U.S. citizens that the administration believes could be used to monitor voter rolls for noncitizens.

The decision means the administration can move ahead with planning for restricting the use of mail ballots even as a lower court continues to weigh the legality of Mr. Trump’s executive order. But with a little more than two months until Election Day — and considerably less time before early voting begins in many states — it remains unclear whether the White House’s rules will be in effect for a midterm election in which control of both chambers is at stake. Additional legal action is a near certainty with the plan’s fate not yet final.

A separate injunction by the same lower court complicates matters. That court action prevents the postal service from implementing some parts of the executive order. That case could also soon be headed to the justices.

Monday’s order from the Supreme Court was unsigned, as is typical in such emergency rulings. The majority wrote that it agreed with the government’s argument that it should be able to move forward with its plans, finding that the Trump administration was “likely to suffer irreparable harm” unless the justices lifted a freeze that had been imposed by lower courts.

The three liberal justices dissented, with Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson warning that the majority “needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections.”

The majority said the states that challenged the president’s order could not demonstrate that they were sufficiently harmed by voting rules that had not yet taken effect. The justices cautioned that their order was preliminary and not a final decision about whether the administration’s order “will necessarily be lawful” once the plans are complete. “On that score, time will tell,” the majority said in the 10-page, unsigned order.

The Supreme Court’s conservative majority has been receptive to some, but not all, of the administration’s broad claims of executive power. In this case, the majority said that the provision of Mr. Trump’s order that required creating lists of U.S. citizens was “an internal directive from the president to a subordinate” and so far imposed no obligations on the states.

Meanwhile, the high court’s order landed just one business day after the Postal Service published final regulations on Friday clarifying how it would carry out the president’s executive order. The Postal Service said in its rule that it would “not take actions to implement the rule specifically for the 2026 election” unless the Supreme Court ruled in the administration’s favor.

A spokesperson for the Postal Service declined to comment, citing the pending lawsuits.

New York Attorney General Letitia James called the ruling a “painful setback,” but predicted it would not be the final word from the court.

“The right to vote is sacred, and no administration should be allowed to put that right in jeopardy by making it harder for eligible voters to cast their ballots,” she said in a statement. “This fight is far from over. We are exploring our legal options.”

In a social media post, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said the court’s decision did not deal with the substance of Mr. Trump’s executive order, asserting that the ruling “does not mean his illegal attempt to restrict mail-in voting will go forward.”

“Donald Trump does not run elections here in Pennsylvania — or in any state,” he added. “We’ll see the Trump Administration in court.”The legal team representing voting rights organizations in the separate challenge to the president’s executive order said in a statement that they were “disappointed by this interim ruling by the Supreme Court,” but would press on with their efforts to block the order.

The team, which includes the American Civil Liberties Union, called the president’s order an “attempt to seize control of election rules from the states and Congress” that was “clearly unconstitutional and unlawful.” They added that they would “continue to vigorously pursue all available avenues to challenge this executive order.”

Mr. Trump signed the executive order in March as part of his broader attempts to curtail voting by mail. It directed federal agencies to create “state citizenship lists” of people who will be 18 or older as of Election Day. Federal officials were then directed to send those names to state election officials, who administer the vote, purportedly so they could use them to purge voter registration lists of anyone who is not a citizen. The order also instructed the Postal Service not to mail ballots on behalf of anyone whose name was not on the approved list.

Several court challenges immediately followed, including a lawsuit in federal court in Massachusetts brought by Democratic state attorneys general. The challengers argued that the president exceeded his authority because the Constitution gives Congress and the states power over elections, not the executive.

In late June, Judge Indira Talwani, a Federal District Court judge in Massachusetts, temporarily blocked the president’s order, finding that it violated the Constitution’s separation of powers. She also determined that Congress had not delegated authority to the Postal Service to determine which voters should receive mail ballots, and that the executive order did not allow enough time before November for the Postal Service to follow the legally required process for agencies when they adopt new rules.

Judge Talwani issued a separate broader ruling in a related case this month, blocking any enforcement of the executive order for the 2026 midterms. She again emphasized that the Constitution does not grant authority over elections to the executive branch. She also noted that, contrary to Mr. Trump’s claims of widespread voter fraud, the government had not provided “evidentiary support of illegal or fraudulent absentee voting.”

A federal appeals court earlier upheld Judge Talwani’s temporary block. At that point, Trump administration lawyers filed an emergency application asking the justices to step in. Several Republican state attorneys general filed a separate, parallel request.

In a brief to the court, the Democratic state attorneys general wrote that the executive order “would allow the federal government to rush out an unprecedented, legally indefensible voter-verification and ballot-interception program that would, among other things, give the U.S. Postal Service far-reaching new powers and responsibilities.”

They also argued that allowing the order to be implemented would mean a chaotic rollout not long before states begin to send out absentee ballots.

And they wrote that voters could be confused and disenfranchised, given that the federal government was likely to make errors in compiling citizen lists and that valid voters would have little time to challenge the government’s determinations.
